assessment.name: Tampa Scale of Kinesiophobia (TSK)
assessment.description: The TSK is a 17-item self report checklist using a 4-point Likert scale that was developed as a measure of fear of movement or (re)injury.

administration.instructions: In these days of high-tech medicine, one of the most important sources of information about you is often missing from your medical records: your own feeling or intuitions about what is happening with your body. We hope that the following information will help to fill that gap. Please answer the following questions according to your true feelings, not according to what others think you should believe. Score each statement from strongly disagree to strong agree by tapping the appropriate box.

rules.label: Total Score
rules.reverse_scoring_handling: Use the printed source values once. Do not reverse again based only on item wording.
rules.coverage: Arithmetic only; diagnostic algorithms, norms and source-specific missing-answer exceptions are not implied.

scoring.coverage: Implemented formulas have explicit item membership and numeric source evidence. Remaining expressions, diagnostic algorithms, percentiles, custom missing-answer policies and interpretation require review.
source_rule_excerpts: Additionally, scores are presented in percentile terms in comparison to patients with chronic back pain (CBP Percentile) and Fibromyalgia (FM Percentile) using data from Roelofs et al (2004). Percentiles are useful to contextualise the respondents score in comparison to typical responses among particular groups. For example, a percentile of 50 compared to the Fibromyalgia sample represents an average level of kinesiophobia compared to others with Fibromyalgia.

A high value on the TSK indicates a high degree of kinesiophobia, and a cutoff score was developed by Vlaeyen (1995), where a score of 37 or over is considered as a high score and are predictive of poorer health outcomes. Use of a total score (including all 17 items) is recommended, although practitioners may wish to interpret results using two subscales.

missing_item_policy.note: Conservative prototype policy, not a claim that the source prohibits prorating. Source exceptions require an explicit reviewed rule.

limitations: Rules do not establish a diagnosis.
No normative percentile is inferred from sample results or approximate distribution data.

source_guidance.title: TSK Scoring & Interpretation
source_guidance.text:
Results consist of a total raw score (range between 17 and 68) and two subscale scores.
Activity Avoidance – this subscale reflects the belief that activity may result in (re)injury or increased pain.
Somatic Focus – reflects the belief in underlying and serious medical problems
Additionally, scores are presented in percentile terms in comparison to patients with chronic back pain (CBP Percentile) and Fibromyalgia (FM Percentile) using data from Roelofs et al (2004). Percentiles are useful to contextualise the respondents score in comparison to typical responses among particular groups. For example, a percentile of 50 compared to the Fibromyalgia sample represents an average level of kinesiophobia compared to others with Fibromyalgia.
A high value on the TSK indicates a high degree of kinesiophobia, and a cutoff score was developed by Vlaeyen (1995), where a score of 37 or over is considered as a high score and are predictive of poorer health outcomes. Use of a total score (including all 17 items) is recommended, although practitioners may wish to interpret results using two subscales.

Additionally, scores are presented in percentile terms in comparison

Thus, a percentile of 50 compared to the Fibromyalgia sample

as low scores. Use of a total score (including all 17 items) is
recommended, although practitioners may wish to interpret results
